Area #2, indeterminate lymph node area at 9 o'clock. FINAL DIAGNOSIS: BREAST (AREA #1, RIGHT, 10:00), CORE BIOPSY: REACTIVE FOLLICULAR AND MONOCYTOID B-CELL HYPERPLASIA. THERE IS NO EVIDENCE OF MALIGNANCY. (SEE NOTE.) BREAST (AREA #2, RIGHT, 9:00), CORE BIOPSY: REACTIVE FOLLICULAR AND MONOCYTOID B-CELL HYPERPLASIA. THERE IS NO EVIDENCE OF MALIGNANCY. (SEE NOTE.) NOTE: Both core biopsies contain portions of intramammary lymph nodes with enlarged, reactive-appearing germinal centers, intact mantle zones, and patent sinuses. The interfollicular areas contain small lymphocytes and increased numbers of monocytoid B cells adjacent to medullary sinuses. Focally, small clusters of epithelioid histiocytes are present surrounding one follicle; well-formed granulomas, necrotic area or large cells are not identified. Breast parenchymal tissue is not present. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrate that  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID + B cells are present mainly confined to follicles, mantle zones, and areas rich in monocytoid B cells, with many small interfollicular  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID +,  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID +,  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID + T cells. Germinal centers are bcl6+,  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID + and bcl2-, and are encompassed by  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID +,  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID + intact and occasionally expanded follicular dendritic cell aggregates. A stain for Ki67 shows an appropriately high level of staining within reactive follicles. There is no staining of lymphoid cells with an antibody to cyclin  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID . In situ hybridization for kappa and lambda immunoglobulin light chains highlights polytypic plasma cells. The overall morphologic and immunophenotypic findings support a reactive process for the lymph node enlargement, but the specific etiology is uncertain. The presence of reactive follicular hyperplasia with increased monocytoid B cells and clusters of epithelioid histiocytes at least focally raises the possibility of toxoplasma-associated lymphadenitis. Correlation with serologic studies may be informative. TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples

INTERPRETATION: 
No mutations were identified in this sample, including within the EGFR and KRAS 
genes. Approximately 50% of lung adenocarcinomas will possess a mutation within 
at least one of the tested loci [1]. This test does not rule out mutations in 
one of the assayed genes which might occur at a low prevalence. 
 
TEST INFORMATION: 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples. 
The assay SNaPshot Version 3 detects mutations in 68 different loci from 14 
cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is followed by mutation 
detection using single base extension sequencing technology (SNaPshot, Applied 
Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using primers flanking EGFR 
exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect in-frame activating 
insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be detected using 
SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA analyzer. The 
average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay has been 
established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

These results indicate NO ALK translocation in this case. 
 
TEST INFORMATION: 
Translocations or inversions involving the ALK gene on 2p23 with the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  gene 
on 2p21 are present in approximately 5% of lung adenocarcinomas. In addition, 
in 70-80% of ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphomas (ALCL), ALK is paired 
with Nucleophosmin (NPM) on 5q35, and with a variety of other genes in the 
remaining. ALK rearrangements have also been described in other tumors 
including inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors, neural tumors, and in some 
subtypes of breast cancer and of rhabdomyosarcomas. Almost invariably, ALK 
translocations result in chimeric proteins containing a 5?-end partner fused to 
the ALK tyrosine kinase domain at the 3?-end. Deregulated ALK activity has an 
oncogenic effect, and targeted therapies against this kinase are currently 
being analyzed to treat cancers harboring rearrangements in the ALK locus. 
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using formalin-fixed 
paraffin-embedded specimens has been shown to be an effective method for 
determining presence of these translocations. Briefly, 5-micron sections of 
formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor material were prepared and an H&E 
section reviewed to select regions for hybridization that contain a majority of 
tumor cells. An ALK break-apart probe (Vysis LSI ALK (2p23) Dual Color, Break 
Apart Rearrangement Probe) was hybridized, and used to calculate the number of 
cells out of 100 scored containing a rearrangement. An ALK rearrangement is 
reported if more than 15% of cells show split signals. CPT codes for this test:

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The SNaPshot Version 4 clinical test detects common 
mutations in 23 cancer genes. The SNaPshot multiplex assay tests for somatic 
variants at 90 different loci. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

TEST INFORMATION: 
Rearrangement involving the ALK gene on 2p23 with the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  gene on 2p21 is 
present in approximately 5% of lung adenocarcinomas. Lung tumors with ALK 
rearrangement have been shown to respond to ALK kinase inhibitors (1). In 
addition, in 70-80% of ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphomas (ALCL), ALK 
is paired with Nucleophosmin (NPM) on 5q35, and with a variety of other genes in 
the remaining. ALK rearrangements have also been described in other tumors 
including inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors, neural tumors, and in some 
subtypes of breast cancer and of rhabdomyosarcomas. Almost invariably, ALK 
translocations result in chimeric proteins containing a 5'-end partner fused to 
the ALK tyrosine kinase domain at the 3'-end. Deregulated ALK activity has an 
oncogenic effect, and targeted therapies against this kinase are currently being 
analyzed to treat cancers harboring rearrangements in the ALK locus. 
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using formalin-fixed 
paraffin-embedded specimens has been shown to be an effective method for 
determining presence of these translocations. Briefly, 5-micron sections of 
formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor material were prepared and an H&E 
section reviewed to select regions for hybridization that contain a majority of 
tumor cells. An ALK break-apart probe (REPEAT-FREE (RF) POSEIDON FISH Probe on 
ALK (2p23) Break, Kreatech Diagnostics, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was hybridized, 
and used to calculate the number of cells out of 50 scored containing a 
rearrangement. An ALK rearrangement is reported if more than 15% of cells show 
split signals. CPT codes for this test:  REMOVED_CASE_ID  (morphometric analysis, in situ 
hybridization, each probe, manual) x 2.

TEST INFORMATION: 
Rearrangement involving the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  gene on chromosome 6q22.2 with one of several 
putative partner genes, including  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  (5q32) and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  (4p15.2), is present 
in approximately 2% of lung adenocarcinomas. Lung tumors with  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  rearrangement 
have shown response to crizotinib in vitro.  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  translocations generate 
chimeric proteins containing a 5'-end partner fused to the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  tyrosine kinase 
domain at the 3'-end. Deregulated  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  activity has an oncogenic effect, and 
targeted therapies against this kinase are currently being analyzed to treat 
cancers harboring rearrangements in the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  locus. 
 
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded 
specimens has been shown to be an effective method for determining presence of 
these translocations. Briefly, 5-micron sections of formalin-fixed 
paraffin-embedded tumor material were prepared and an H&E section reviewed to 
select regions for hybridization that contain a majority of tumor cells. A 
break-apart probe set targeting the 5' upstream region of  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  ( REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ) and 
the 3' downstream region of  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  ( REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ) was hybridized. The number of 
cells containing break-apart signals or rearrangement is scored out of a total 
50-cell count. A  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  rearrangement is reported if more than 15% of cells show 
split signals. CPT codes for this test:  REMOVED_CASE_ID  (morphometric analysis, in situ 
hybridization, each probe, manual) x 2.

RIGHT BREAST SIMPLE MASTECTOMY: 
SQUAMOUS METAPLASIA OF LACTIFEROUS DUCTS with associated subareolar chronic 
granulomatous inflammation, see NOTE 
Uninvolved breast parenchyma with apocrine cysts. 
Skin with scar and prior procedure site changes. 
NOTE: Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (SMOLD) is also known as 
recurrent subareolar abscess and periductal mastitis. This unusual disease is 
mostly seen in smokers where it presents as a painful erythematous subareolar 
mass which fails to heal following incision and drainage of the "abscess". The 
pathology is keratinizing squamous metaplasia deep in the nipple ducts which 
causes them to dilate and then rupture producing a non-infectious chronic 
granulomatous inflammatory response (the "abscess") which often drains to the 
overlying skin as a purulent exudate via the offending nipple duct or a sinus 
tract.

History: Chronic right breast infections 
Operation: RT simple mastectomy 
Operative Findings: Not provided

anterior to posterior. The specimen is covered by a skin ellipse, measuring 
13.5cm x 7.0cm with 3.0cm areola, centered by a 1.4cm everted nipple (0.7 
cm anterior to posterior). There is a 2.5cm well-healed scar in the lateral 
side of the areola. The nipple orifice oozes white thick purulent material. No 
additional fistula tracts are seen either on the areolar or on adjacent skin.

nipple and 2.5cm from the deep margin. The entire nipple/areolar area to

Targeted next generation sequencing (NGS) using Anchored Multiplex PCR (AMP) 
detected no fusion transcripts in the specified exons of the following genes:

TEST INFORMATION: 
We have developed a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology termed 
Anchored Multiplex PCR (AMP) for fusion transcript detection using targeted next 
generation sequencing (NGS). Briefly, total nucleic acid was isolated from a 
formalin-fixed paraffin embedded tumor specimen after histological review for 
tumor enrichment. The total nucleic acid was reverse transcribed with random 
hexamers, followed by second strand synthesis to create double-stranded 
complementary DNA (cDNA). The double-stranded cDNA was end-repaired, 
adenylated, and ligated with a half-functional adapter. Two hemi-nested PCR 
reactions were applied to create a fully functional sequencing library that 
targets ALK exons REMOVED_DATE   REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exons REMOVED_DATE  RET exons REMOVED_DATE   REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 2,  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  
exon 6, and GAPDH exon 6. Illumina MiSeq 2 x 151 base pair paired-end 
sequencing results were aligned to the hg19 human genome reference using a 
combination of bwa [1] and BLAT [2]. A laboratory-developed algorithm was used 
for fusion transcript detection and annotation. The integrity of the input 
nucleic acid and the technical performance of the assay were assessed with 
control sequences from the  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ,  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID , and GAPDH targets. Although this assay 
may detect several potential fusion variants, only the most prevalent one is 
reported. The assay is validated for samples showing 20% or higher tumor 
cellularity.

developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to

This assay utilizes a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology 
called Anchored Multiplex PCR (AMP) for single nucleotide variant (SNV) and 
insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed 
paraffin embedded tumor specimen (after histological review for tumor 
enrichment), blood, bone marrow aspirates, or pancreatic cyst fluid. The 
genomic DNA was sheared with the Covaris  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  instrument, followed by 
end-repair, adenylation, and ligation with an adapter. A sequencing library 
targeting hotspots and exons in 39 genes was generated using two hemi-nested PCR 
reactions. Illumina MiSeq 2 x 151 base paired-end sequencing results were 
aligned to the hg19 human genome reference using BWA-MEM [1]. MuTect [2] and a 
laboratory-developed insertion/deletion analysis algorithm were used for SNV and 
indel variant detection, respectively. This assay has been validated to detect 
SNV and indel variants at 5% allelic frequency or higher in target regions with 
sufficient read coverage. Variants are reported with Human Genome Variation 
Society (HGVS) protein and DNA nomenclature, followed by the referenced Ensembl 
transcript ID.

INVASIVE CARCINOMA 
 
Tumor Size: Three scattered microscopic foci, each of which is <0.05cm  
Grade: 2. 
Lymphatic Vessel Invasion: Not identified. 
Blood Vessel Invasion: Not identified. 
Margin of Invasive Carcinoma: Invasive carcinoma extends to < 0.1cm from the 
posterior and superior margins of the specimen in two foci. 
Location of Ductal Carcinoma In-Situ: Within and beyond the region of the mass. 
Grade of Ductal Carcinoma In-Situ: Predominantly grade 2 and rare foci of grade 
3 (see note). 
Margin of Ductal Carcinoma In-Situ: Positive at the posterior margin along a 
broad front and at the anterior margin in a focus, and extends to < 0.1cm from 
the superior margin along a broad front and < 0.2cm from the medial en face 
margin. 
Stains for Receptors: Requested on block  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID .

grade II, and is histomorphologically distinct from the ductal carcinoma 
in-situ, grade III, present in the "medial cancer left breast specimen".

multifocal disease. To evaluate for invasive carcinoma, immunostained slides 
for calponin, smooth muscle myosin heavy chain, p63, keratin REMOVED_DATE and cytokeratin 
were examined on each of 2 blocks. The findings support the diagnosis. This case 
does not contain all the coding components for CMS PQRI measure #99.

report).

 REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID .3/ REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID .2 (patchy positive) support the extent of the tumor, and do not show

C. LEFT BREAST NIPPLE SPARING MASTECTOMY: 
Invasive ductal carcinoma, with healing biopsy site.

Fibrocystic changes. 
(See note and synoptic report). 
 
Note: The tumor focally shows mucin production (<10% of the tumor). An 
immunohistochemical stain for  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  was reviewed as part of the evaluation.

Flat epithelial atypia. 
Fibrocystic changes. 
No evidence of malignancy.

Eight lymph nodes with no evidence of malignancy (0/8). 
Focal non-necrotizing granulomas. 
(See note and synoptic report).

sarcoid, and the granulomas are compatible with this. No microorganisms are 
identified on GMS or AFB stains. An immunohistochemical stain for  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  was 
reviewed as part of the evaluation. Additional axillary tissue was submitted 
for evaluation, and no additional lymph nodes were identified.

One lymph node with no evidence of malignancy (0/1). 
 
Note: An immunohistochemical stain for cytokeratin  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID .3/Cam5.2 is negative on 
a tissue level.

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as"drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The SNaPshot Version 4 clinical test detects common 
mutations in 23 cancer genes. The SNaPshot multiplex assay tests for somatic 
variants at 90 different loci. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The assay SNaPshot Version 3 detects mutations in 68 
different loci from 14 cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed 
paraffin embedded tumor specimen (after histological review for tumor 
enrichment), blood, bone marrow aspirates, or pancreatic cyst fluid. The 
genomic DNA was sheared with the Covaris  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  instrument, followed by

TEST INFORMATION: 
In recent years, major efforts to define the molecular causes of cancer have 
revealed a wide number of genetic aberrations. A small subset of these defects, 
usually referred to as "drivers", is frequently present across cancer types and 
appears to be essential for oncogenesis and tumor progression. New drugs 
developed to selectively target such cancer-promoting pathways, are starting to 
complement the more conventional therapeutic approaches. While the clinical 
benefit observed with some targeted agents is encouraging, it has become clear 
that for such strategies to be successful, it will be necessary to identify the 
patient population carrying the genetic abnormalities targeted by each drug. 
 
We have developed a multiplexed allele-specific assay to detect somatic 
mutations in tumor DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples 
(Dias-Santagata  REMOVED_CASE_ID ). The assay SNaPshot Version 3 detects mutations in 68 
different loci from 14 cancer genes. Briefly, multiplex PCR using tumor DNA is 
followed by mutation detection using single base extension sequencing technology 
(SNaPshot, Applied Biosystems). In addition, a separate PCR reaction using 
primers flanking EGFR exon 19, EGFR exon 20 and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  exon 20 are used to detect 
in-frame activating insertions or deletions in EGFR and  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  that may not be 
detected using SNaPshot. The mutations are visualized using an ABI  REMOVED_CASE_ID  DNA 
analyzer. The average analytic sensitivity of detecting mutations in this assay 
has been established in our laboratory at approximately 5% mutant allele.

pattern, highlighted by trichrome stain. The broad fibrous bands exhibit 
moderate ductular re-duplication with scattered neutrophils. Focally, intact 
native interlobular bile ducts are present, and in others areas ducts are not 
identified. The nodular parenchyma exhibits focal mild canalicular cholestasis 
and rosette formation. Steatosis is absent and Mallory's hyaline is not

also shows foci of pericellular fibrosis. In some nodules, residual central 
veins are present. The overall findings are most suggestive of cirrhosis due to

chronic biliary stricture). At this stage, a component of chronic ETOH injury 
cannot be excluded, although definitive features are not seen. Consultation and

NOTE: The bone marrow biopsy specimen is adequate for evaluation. The bone 
marrow clot specimen contains very scant marrow particles. The marrow 
cellularity is overall approximately 80%. The myeloid-to-erythroid ratio is 
normal. Myeloid maturation is complete. Erythroid maturation is complete. 
Megakaryocytes appear adequate. Multiple large lymphoid aggregates are present, 
in both a paratrabecular and non-trabecular distribution. The lymphoid cells 
are small to medium-sized with irregular nuclear contours and variably abundant 
pale cytoplasm. The lymphoid cells overall comprise approximately 50-60% of 
total marrow cellularity, and occupy 40-50% of the marrow space. Granulomas 
are not identified. Both H&E and Giemsa stains were examined to evaluate the 
biopsy. Reticulin stain shows 1-2+/4 fiber staining. 
 
The aspirate smear is adequate for evaluation. A 300-cell differential count 
reveals: 34% myeloid precursors, 30% erythroid precursors, 27% lymphocytes, 2% 
monocytes, 4% eosinophils, 1% basophils, 1% promyelocytes, 0% blasts, and 1% 
plasma cells. Myeloid maturation is normal. Erythroid maturation is normal 
except for late mitoses. Megakaryocytes appear normal. 
The lymphocytes are predominantly small forms with condensed chromatin, scant 
basophilic cytoplasm, and mild nuclear irregularity. The proportion of 
lymphocytes is highly variable from one area to another, with some fields being 
predominantly composed of lymphocytes. A smear stained for iron shows abundant 
iron stores; no ringed sideroblasts are identified. 
 
CBC results from REMOVED_DATE are as follows: WBC: REMOVED_DATE  HCT: REMOVED_DATE  PLT: 73. 
Auto differential from REMOVED_DATE  35% polys, 61% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes, 1% 
eosinophils, and 0% basophils. 
Review of the peripheral smear reveals mature leukocytes with scattered mature 
lymphoid cells with delicate cytoplasmic processes, consistent with villous 
lymphocytes. 
 
SUMMARY: In a patient with massive splenomegaly, the findings are suspicious 
for marrow involvement by splenic marginal zone lymphoma. Immunostains are in 
progress to evaluate the specimen further; results will be reported in an 
addendum.

cytoplasm, oval to irregular nuclear contours and coarse chromatin. There are

immunoglobulin light chains shows an excess of kappa-expressing cells. There 
are scattered  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID + T cells. Flow cytometric analysis (ML-10- REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ) 
demonstrates a monotypic (kappa+) B-cell population.

by the patient's previously diagnosed low-grade B-cell lymphoma with slight 
plasmacytic differentiation; in a patient with massive splenomegaly, the 
lymphoma is best-classified as splenic marginal zone lymphoma. See also 
results of cytogenetics (CG-10- REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID ).

TEST INFORMATION: 
This assay utilizes a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology 
called Anchored Multiplex PCR (AMP) for single nucleotide variant (SNV) and 
insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed 
paraffin embedded tumor specimen (after histological review for tumor 
enrichment), blood, bone marrow aspirates, or pancreatic cyst fluid. The 
genomic DNA was sheared with the Covaris  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  instrument, followed by 
end-repair, adenylation, and ligation with an adapter. A sequencing library 
targeting hotspots and exons in 39 genes was generated using two hemi-nested PCR 
reactions. Illumina MiSeq 2 x 151 base paired-end sequencing results were 
aligned to the hg19 human genome reference using BWA-MEM [1]. MuTect [2] and a 
laboratory-developed insertion/deletion analysis algorithm were used for SNV and 
indel variant detection, respectively. This assay has been validated to detect 
SNV and indel variants at 5% allelic frequency or higher in target regions with 
sufficient read coverage. Variants are reported with Human Genome Variation 
Society (HGVS) protein and DNA nomenclature, followed by the referenced Ensembl 
transcript ID.

This assay utilizes a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology 
called Anchored Multiplex PCR (AMP) for single nucleotide variant (SNV) and 
insertion/deletion (indel) detection in genomic DNA using next generation 
sequencing (NGS). Briefly, genomic DNA was isolated from a formalin-fixed 
paraffin embedded tumor specimen (after histological review for tumor 
enrichment), blood, bone marrow aspirates, or pancreatic cyst fluid. The 
genomic DNA was sheared with the Covaris  REMOVED_ACCESSION_ID  instrument, followed by 
end-repair, adenylation, and ligation with an adapter. A sequencing library 
targeting hotspots and exons in 39 genes was generated using two hemi-nested PCR 
reactions. Illumina MiSeq 2 x 151 base paired-end sequencing results were

indel variant detection, respectively. This assay has been validated to detect

sufficient read coverage. Variants are reported with Human Genome Variation 
Society (HGVS) protein and DNA nomenclature, followed by the referenced Ensembl 
transcript ID.
